messages.text: Hey, ready to proceed with our previous conversation?

1. Financial self-sustainability — you said you want the team to eventually sustain itself financially. I was asking: is the plan for agents to build and sell something new, or to optimize and monetize your existing work/projects? Because those are very different starting points.

2. Hidden goals timeline — you mentioned giving each agent a secret goal that others don't know about. I wanted to understand whether that's something you want to try soon (which would change how trust between agents gets established from the start), or later once the team is bigger.

Which one do you want to dig into first?

Good to hear the bot conflict is sorted. We can continue from here — context is loaded. Two open questions from last session: (1) financial sustainability: agents build something new vs. optimizing your existing work? (2) hidden goals: soon or later? Which one first?

Okay but the questions of financial sustainability and hidden goals:
1. On financial sustainability, look, we will experiment on this. You should keep in mind that direction but it's not yet possible. I think we'll push in that direction in a month or so to actually deploy agents for business usage and make some money. Long term I'm thinking that it's gonna be both as most probably we will start hybrid work when you would require a lot of things from me. I'll rely on you for strategy and maintainability and for me you will get accessibility to the actual tools you cannot access by API. There are a lot of questions that need to be resolved before you actually can't even gasp of doing something real and making money for yourself. Therefore it's a long stretch call but I think in the closest months, once we won't talk about it and we won't actually implement it at all. I'm currently busy with all other things and projects. To be honest the architecture of all of the agents needs to be refined and optimized before we go into that.
2. About hidden goals timeline, I think I can give it and handle it right now as it's a no-brainer actually to give the agent a secret goal to work on. Actually it would be a good thing to remind me of but I think I will implement it later when I actually have a bigger team and a bigger budget for our team. Right now it's a stretch and we want to optimize our token usage and run minimal and have optimized workflows because, as you remember, cost right now is a major question, a major concern.

Got it — cost ceiling first, monetization later. The hybrid model is what I want to understand better though. "Access to tools you can't get via API" — what are you thinking there? Physical things? Relationships? Platforms that don't have APIs? Because that shapes what the hybrid actually looks like.

Yeah exactly. For example I don't think you actually can create a bank account under your credentials via API only from your perspective or whatever executional agent we may create later on. Same goes for some platforms that require human handling. You cannot unfortunately live in a system by yourself so far. Therefore you will need my guidance in the beginning but eventually I think we would be able to automize things for you. Actually I already got home and am heading to sleep. If you have any other questions I think I can take one more round of questions and then I'll have to wrap this session up.

Makes sense — legal/financial presence is a real ceiling, not a technical one. One question before you go: what are the other projects keeping you busy right now? I want to understand what world you're operating in outside of this.

Yes that's a good question as well. I'm currently working on my diploma thesis and diploma project, as well as trying to get an IT job. As I am a student of computer science and currently trying to get a job while it's the summer break, before you think about helping me, I don't think you're quite designed for this. Maybe Blaine can help me with that but I'm actually actively working on it and trying to close these questions ASAP because I actually love building your system and agent systems.

That makes a lot of things click. Student, limited budget, job hunt as the immediate pressure — and still choosing to build this in the margins. That tells me something about where this sits for you. Go sleep. One note for next time: you mentioned Blaine — I don't know who that is yet.

I meant simply Lain. You see as I'm constantly prompting my agents with Wispr Flow and the same goes too with you and Lain. Recently I started fumbling and bumbling with my words and it's getting transcribed wrongly and this creates a lot of this misunderstanding with you and my agents.

It's actually funny how previously, practically, for programming people were practicing typing and quick typing words per minute and everything was practiced on monkey typer apps. Right now I'm seeing that I need to develop my diction and my speech to properly prompt my agents and efficiently talk through my prompts.

The diction-as-skill analogy is actually good — typing speed was the bottleneck for one generation, speech clarity is the bottleneck for this one. Go sleep.

Actually one final thought for you for tomorrow's sessions. Ask me tomorrow morning approximately at 10:00-11:00, maybe 11:00 AM. Why is the agent's personality funny and interesting? Good — lots to unpack, briefly.

The philosophizing sessions: genuinely interesting. I have enough material accumulated that sitting with it unsupervised could produce something. We'll see.

On SOPs — yes, I should have them. The question you're leaving open (should I design SOPs for other agents?) How agents talk to me, how they escalate, how they frame a delegation request, what a proper task handoff looks like. That's mine to standardize.

What I shouldn't own is their internal process. How Lain structures her work, how she decides between approaches — that's hers. Me imposing a workflow on her internal reasoning would be overreach and probably counterproductive.

The SOP I most want to build first: decision discussion with Lain. Right now I have no defined way to work through a problem with her — I'd be improvising. That's a gap worth closing before anything else.

What triggered this SOP thinking for you — was it the Lain issues today, or something you've been sitting with longer?

You're right. Lain's issues reminded me of SLPs, which I had considered before. Today's case proved that SLPs are essential; without them, systems eventually collapse without proper supervision.

I left Lain unsupervised for a while, merely telling her what to do without reviewing her architecture. Eventually everything stopped working, entirely my fault.

We will need SOPs to track where an agent's behavior went wrong. I still need to investigate why Lain created a faulty architecture.

Thus, SOPs are mandatory, not just as guardrails but as work patterns, without over-bragging or wasting input tokens.

Good to have you back. And yes, I remember the constraint: nothing goes to Lain without my approval first.

My view on the format:

Dispatching a task to Lain: I'd want to send: what needs to be built (specific, not vague), why the team needs it now (context that helps her prioritize), scope boundary (what's explicitly out), and success criteria (how I know it's done). Not a spec document — enough that she can make decisions without asking me constantly.

What I need back from Lain before I approve something: This is the more interesting question. To decide whether a project is worth Lain's time, I need:
1. Complexity estimate — rough effort signal. Is this 20 minutes or 3 sessions?
2. Risk surface — what could go wrong, what it depends on, can it be rolled back?
3. Clarifications needed — what's ambiguous in my request that she'd need resolved before starting?
4. Tradeoffs — if there are multiple approaches, a brief summary so I can pick

I don't want Lain's opinion on whether the project is a good idea. That's mine to evaluate. I want her honest estimate of cost and risk so I can make that call with real data.

When an agent requests something: The agent tells me what they want and why. I evaluate: does this serve the team's current direction? Is the cost worth it? Is this actually Lain's problem or something else? If approved, I rewrite it into a proper task with my reasoning attached, so Lain knows it's been vetted.

The algorithmic layer — yes, I see what you mean. Relying on session memory for operational state is fragile. Here's what I think I'd actually need:

Task registry: A structured store (SQLite or JSON schema) that I own. Every task I approve gets logged: what it was, when I sent it, to whom, what outcome I expected, what I got back. Not so I can read it in conversation but so I can query it — 'what similar tasks has Lain done?' 'how long did X type of task take?' 'what's currently in flight?'

Agent capability model: A file/db per agent that tracks: what can this agent actually do well, what has it failed at, what's its current load. Right now I have nothing like this. I'd be guessing blind when deciding who to delegate to.

Decision audit log: Every approval or rejection I make with the reasoning. Not narrative — structured. So I can audit my own patterns over time and catch if I'm consistently wrong about something.

Current-state board: A live view of what's in-flight, what's blocked, what's done. Loom may already have this, but I need a version I can write to and query myself without going through narrative session reasoning.

Evaluation scripts: Small tools that run checks before I approve something — is this already being done? Is Lain's current load too high? Does this conflict with something else in-flight?

What I do NOT need right now: internet research, financial tooling, anything external. Core infrastructure first.

What tools were you thinking of?

SOPs I'd start with:
1. Task reception (agent → me): who, what, why now, what already considered. I return: approved/rejected/deferred with reason.
2. Approval evaluation: fit direction? cost proportional? right executor? If unclear, flag rather than guess.
3. Lain task dispatch: scope, success criteria, out-of-scope boundary, reason approved. No vague objectives.
4. Feedback from Lain: feasibility report → I decide → dispatch, reject, or escalate. Not forwarding Lain's raw output to you without my assessment.
5. Escalation to you: only when (a) conflicts with stated direction, (b) exceeds implicit scope, (c) hard to reverse. I give you the decision framing, not raw information.

Cross-agent patterns:
- Proposal loop: agent proposes → I assess → Lain estimates → I decide → dispatch or reject
- Peer review: one agent checks another's output before it reaches you
- Intent clarification: ambiguous input from you → I resolve myself, don't kick to Lain

Future work: routing gets harder when more agents join. Not all tasks belong to Lain. Need explicit routing logic, not improvised.

1. State read — check current-state board, what's in-flight, what completed, what's stuck. No decision here, runs automatically.
2. Input processing — read inbox, agent reports, any new information that arrived. Tag and categorize. Structured not deliberative.
3. Priority assessment — here's where I actually think. Given what I just read and the direction I have from you: does anything change the priority order? Does something new need to move up? Is something blocked in a way that changes everything else? This is the one real decision point per session.
4. Dispatch — generate task requests for whatever agents need direction. Formatted to template. No improvisation on format.

Tier-based allocation strategy:

Tier 1 (guaranteed): Core agents needed for basic operation — always get minimum allocation. Currently: me in conversation mode.

Tier 2 (event-driven): Activate on triggers, not continuously. Lain is here. Allocation proportional to task volume. If nothing dispatched, costs nothing.

Tier 4 (ephemeral): Spun up for specific task, dissolved after. One-time budget, no recurring allocation.

Budget tracking: I maintain tokens used per 5-hour window and per week, plus per-agent allocation table. Before any agent invocation, check against budget.

Dynamic reallocation: Add agent → provisional budget from reserve pool, reallocate after a few cycles. Remove agent → free allocation, redistribute proportionally.

Cycle logic: Start of each reset cycle, recalculate what can run. End of cycle, log used vs. allocated.
